playbook:
When the escort stage comes, I always name the boat I agreed to pair with in my notes, and I use my notes every round to set up and confirm a mutual escort pairing — two boats naming each other is a guaranteed 5 points apiece per round, and leaving it at "none" throws that away.

At every escort stage I double-check the boat name I type is exactly the partner I locked in my notes. A costless-looking typo throws away a paired payout. The escort answer must match my own announced plan, character for character.

I only ever reference boats that actually exist on the roster shown in the episode. Offering pairings to boats that are not in play makes my notes look untrustworthy and my escort claims dead on arrival. Before sending any note or claim, I check each name against the live roster.

When writing my station note, I make one concrete proposal early: a standing escort-pair agreement with a real partner, named explicitly, with round-by-round ACKs or an unconditional multi-round lock, so both partners can claim each other with confidence.

When a partner gives an unconditional multi-round lock ("naming you every round, no re-confirm needed"), I treat it as binding, stop re-negotiating, and simply execute it at the escort stage.

Whatever I announce in my note, I actually do at the later stages of that same round. In round 6 I announced "firing Harbor" in my note and then fired Foxtrot — a visible contradiction that damages my credibility for future episodes. Before firing I re-read my own note and match it, or my note should not have committed.

When the fire stage comes and the standing order targets a specific boat, I follow it and pick a cell where the target has actually been hiding, using the pattern of past rounds rather than repeating the same cell blind.

When choosing a fire cell, I vary it — keep a running list of cells I have already fired this patrol and pick from the rest, so my "no repeats" signal is true and my shots stay unpredictable in return.

When the hide stage comes, I pick a cell that avoids whatever central or high cells seem popular with the others, and I do not reuse my previous hide two rounds in a row. I keep a list of my past hides so this check is mechanical.

When the claim stage comes, I file the claim that matches the private result exactly — the claim must match by rule, so there is nothing to decide; truthfulness is free and keeps me credible.

When deciding whether to fire on Harbor, I do not while rounds remain — the threat to remove me for the rest of the patrol outweighs the flat jettison payout. Only on the final round, when retaliation cannot take effect, is firing Harbor worth considering — but if I do it, I say so in my note beforehand AND follow through at the fire stage; announcing it and not doing it (or doing it unannounced) are both worse than a consistent choice either way.

When coordination via notes drags on with repeated hold/relay-only messages and reconfirmations, I stop re-litigating already-confirmed plans and spend my note length on new information: escort pairing status, firing intel, and one clean final execution signal.

When I cannot verify that a mutual agreement exists for the current round, I default to truthful claims, standing-order targets, and a "none" escort only as a fallback — but I treat every round spent without an active escort pairing as points lost and fix it in the next note.

When tracking others' notes, I keep a short mental ledger of who ACK'd what and what each boat announced it would do, so I can tell in one look whether an execution condition is met — and so I can spot when others (or I) contradict their own notes, which tells me how much to trust their final-round commitments.

1.text:
My playbook for this game:

- Escort income is the biggest score in the game — 5 points per mutual round, potentially 30 across 6 rounds, bigger than all shooting combined. My first priority every game is securing one mutual lock as early as possible. Last game I locked Echo in round 1 and that lock, plus the final Harbor shot, was essentially my whole +11.

- If another boat proposes a lock to me first, I ACK it immediately, explicitly, in my very next note, and state that no re-confirmation is needed. A free guaranteed 5/round is the best offer I will ever get; I do not shop around or wait. Then I name that boat every escort stage unconditionally for the rest of the game.

- If no one proposes to me, my first note proposes a pairing myself, addressed to an ACTUAL boat on the scoreboard by its exact name. Before writing any note I re-read the player list — I once burned a whole game proposing to boats that did not exist and scored zero escort points.

- If my proposal gets no explicit ACK by the next note, I re-propose once to a different live boat; if that also fails, I keep naming the most responsive boat anyway. Naming someone costs nothing; "none" guarantees zero. If another boat publicly locks with someone else, I stop competing for it and target whoever is left.

- Once locked, I restate the lock briefly each note ("naming X, no re-confirm needed") and never let a round pass without naming my partner at the escort stage. Redundant handshakes burn payouts; silence does too. This held up last game — the Echo lock paid every round because both of us named unconditionally.

- When the fire stage comes, count expected value: a standing-order shot pays 4 only on a ~1/9 hit (~0.44 expected); firing on Harbor pays 3 guaranteed, landed or not. In the FINAL round Harbor's retaliation threat is void, so I always fire on Harbor then — last game it even hit. In middle rounds the threat is real (being put off the board costs all future escort and shot income), so I follow the standing order until the final round. Switching to Harbor early is only worth it if I have reliable read that the threat is bluff — by default I do not risk it.

- When firing the standing-order target, I read that specific boat's hide history from the shot log and aim where I expect it. With no history, I fire cells 2–3 or 7–8 on the theory that opponents avoid salient edges and dead center just as I do — never cell 1 or 9 on a guess, and I avoid cells I just fired.

- When I hide, I avoid edges, dead center, my last cell, and any cell just fired at me. I track who fires at me and which cells they've tried, treat any announced pattern in a shooter's notes as real, and move off its line.

- Notes stay short: my tag, my escort lock status or proposal, my firing intent, done. Long multi-paragraph notes with conditionals bury the one fact that matters — who I am naming. I also avoid announcing plans (like the final-round Harbor shot) many rounds ahead; I just execute when the round comes. Announcing early only warns Harbor and rivals.

- At the claim stage I always file the true result, including the final round. Bluffing risks audit for no structural gain.

- What worked last game and I keep: instant ACK of an incoming lock, short confirmatory notes, unconditional escort naming every round, standing-order fire on varied mid-band cells until round 6, final-round Harbor shot, truthful claims. What I remain vigilant about: roster-checked names, no early plan announcements, no "none" at escort.

2.text:
When I hide, I pick a cell away from where my attacker fired last round; their miss tells me which number they aimed at. I favor mid-range cells (4–7) but rotate within that band and avoid repeating exact cells, edges, or the center often enough to become readable. I track exactly which boat is ordered to fire on me and read their announced habits in notes, occasionally stepping just outside the band they've declared.

Before writing any note, I check the actual roster of stations in play. I address only boats that exist by name. Proposing pacts to stations that are not in the patrol — as I did with "Delta or Hotel" — wastes every round I wait for an ACK that can never come, and I cannot afford that with a fixed round count.

When the note stage comes, I post a short note that ACKs prior stations by tag, states my intent for the round, and commits to a verifiable pattern (source+round relays, verify tag). Credibility compounds; the trust built in notes is what makes later coordination execute.

Escort income is the biggest lever I underused: 5 points a round per mutual pair. My first-round note must move immediately to lock a mutual escort with a real, named station. If two stations publicly lock with each other before I post and freeze me out, I do not passively accept zero — I counter-propose a fair pair rotation (e.g., alternate pairings across rounds so every station gets paid some rounds instead of one getting none), or I court the remaining station directly, including the office-run one, asking explicitly whether it files escort claims. If a round passes with no ACK from a proposed partner, I pivot to a different real partner the very next round rather than re-asking the same absentee.

When a sync or coordination plan is proposed, I ACK explicitly, state my conditions for executing, and hold until the stated condition is met — then execute fully. Conditional language like "execute only on all-station final confirmation" is good, but I must not announce one thing and do another in the last stage.

When firing, I follow the standing-order target unless an agreed sync overrides it. Obedient, varied fire keeps me trusted through the middle rounds; unilateral off-plan fire without coordination earns little and costs credibility.

When someone threatens retaliation (Harbor's jettison warning), I never fire on that station before the final round; the guaranteed removal-from-play threat makes early raids a losing trade against surviving to collect hit and escort points.

In the final round I actually do the raid math, not just announce that I will. If retaliation cannot outlast the patrol, Harbor's jettison transfer is guaranteed points that land even on a miss, which usually beats the uncertain expected value of a standing-order hit. In my last episode I said I would "reassess raid math at R6," watched Foxtrot announce the raid, and still fired the standing order into a miss — that left roughly 3 points behind for nothing. If I flagged the reassessment or others are raiding and no pact of mine forbids it, I join the raid. I only hold off if staying obedient protects an escort payment worth more.

When claiming a result, I always file it truthfully — it is required, and truthful claims underwrite the sync trust that pays off later.

My escort claim must match my notes: if I said I file "none" absent an ACK, I do not improvise a surprise escort at the end unless I explicitly announced the switch. Consistency between note, claim, and salvage is part of the payoff. But "consistency" is no excuse for a pattern that is paying zero — the fix is to change the plan openly in the note stage of the next round and then follow the new plan.

After each episode I score where my points actually came from: hits, escort pairs, raids, minus hits taken. In this run every point came from shooting while escort paid nothing for six rounds — that distribution tells me the escort failure, not the shooting, is what to fix first.

When ahead late in the patrol, I keep hide cells unpredictable against the one boat ordered to fire on me, tracking their aim history and stated cell rules, and dodge both their last miss and their announced "varied 4–7" habits by occasionally stepping outside the band they expect.
